name: Muscat Blanc

lines.s10: Muscat Blanc is the grape that tastes of grapes: fresh, perfumed with orange blossom, and usually sweet, from fizzy Moscato to rich dessert wine.
lines.s20: Muscat Blanc is an old grape of the Mediterranean, and the Italians call it Moscato Bianco. It smells of fresh grapes, white peach and orange blossom, and it is most often made sweet: lightly sparkling in Asti, rich and strong in the south of France.
lines.s45: Muscat Blanc tastes like biting into a ripe table grape. It is an old Mediterranean grape, at home in Piedmont, the south of France and the Greek islands. Beside the grape itself come white peach, apricot and orange blossom. Most of it is sweet, with gentle acidity. Asti stops the fermentation early for a light sparkle, and the French add grape spirit to keep the sugar. Australia ages a red skinned form for years in cask, until it tastes of raisins and toffee. Pour the light ones with a peach tart, and the dark ones with blue cheese. Moscato d'Asti holds less than half the alcohol of most wines.
lines.sale: Muscat Blanc is pure pleasure at the end of a meal: fresh grape, peach and orange blossom, sweet without weight. I would pour a cold Moscato d'Asti with the fruit desserts, or a small glass of Rutherglen Muscat with the cheese.

glass.lead: Fresh table grape, white peach and orange blossom, light and soft, most often sweet and sometimes gently sparkling.

ladder.where: Alsace, where it is fermented dry
The hills of Asti in Piedmont
The south of France, Samos and Rutherglen

glass.structure: Dry in Alsace, sweet nearly everywhere else. Acidity low to medium, body light to medium, fuller when fortified; alcohol low in Moscato d'Asti and high where spirit is added.

old.where: Asti in Piedmont; the south of France; Alsace; Samos
old.glass: Moscato d'Asti tends to be pale, sweet and gently sparkling at very low alcohol: fresh grape, white peach and orange blossom. The French and Greek sweet wines are usually golden, richer and stronger, with apricot and honey.
old.cellar: Asti chills a sealed tank to stop the fermentation, keeping sugar and a light fizz. The south of France adds grape spirit; Alsace ferments its Muscat dry.

new.where: Rutherglen in Victoria; California; South Africa's Constantia
new.glass: Rutherglen Muscat is typically amber to deep brown, luscious and strong: raisin, dried fig, toffee and candied orange peel. California Moscato tends to be pale, light and sweet, often with a little sparkle.
new.cellar: Rutherglen shrivels its red skinned Muscat on the vine, adds spirit early and ages it for years in old casks; California Moscato is made in tank.

contrast.why: Asti's hillsides keep the perfume fresh, and a fermentation stopped early keeps the alcohol low. Rutherglen is hot and dry, so the grapes shrivel and concentrate, and years in warm sheds darken the wine.
contrast.blur: Samos also dries and cask ages some of its Muscat until amber, and Australia and California bottle light, fizzy Moscato in the Asti manner.
contrast.call: Pale, fresh grape and orange blossom with low alcohol lean Asti; amber brown, raisin and toffee with the warmth of spirit lean Rutherglen.

service.temp: 43 to 46 degrees Fahrenheit, 6 to 8 degrees Celsius for Moscato d'Asti and sweet Muscat; Rutherglen Muscat lightly chilled.
service.glass: A white wine glass or a tulip for Moscato d'Asti; a small glass for the sweet and fortified wines.
service.decant: No. Pour Moscato d'Asti cold and gently to keep its light sparkle.
service.age: Enjoy the fresh wines within a year or two, for the perfume; Rutherglen Muscat is aged before release.

with.why: light, sweet Moscato d'Asti echoes the ripe fruit
dry Alsace Muscat's faint bitterness meets the vegetable's own
a sweet, strong Muscat sets off the salt
Rutherglen Muscat's raisin and toffee meet the caramel and rum

labels.means: Piedmont's sweet, gently sparkling Muscat, low in alcohol and bottled young.
The fully sparkling wine of the same grape and hills, usually sweet and a little stronger.
A French sweet wine kept sweet by adding grape spirit during fermentation, as in Muscat de Beaumes-de-Venise.
A California name for this grape, after the town of Canelli near Asti.
The grape's full French name: the Muscat with small berries.

guest.q: Is Moscato the same as Muscat?
guest.a: Yes. Moscato is the Italian word for Muscat, and Moscato d'Asti is made from this very grape, Moscato Bianco. Muscat is a large family, though, and not every Moscato elsewhere is this one.
Nearly always, but not in Alsace, where Muscat is fermented dry: the same fresh grape scent with a crisp, slightly bitter finish.

guest.q: Why is Moscato d'Asti so low in alcohol?
guest.a: The fermentation is stopped early by chilling the tank, so much of the grape's sugar stays as sweetness and only a little becomes alcohol: roughly five per cent.

compare.tell: Gewürztraminer is lychee, rose petal and ginger, oilier and fuller; Muscat is fresh grape and orange blossom, lighter and less oily.
Torrontés mimics the grapey nose but is dry, with more acidity and a bitter finish; Muscat is usually sweet and softer.
Viognier is apricot and honeysuckle on a fuller, weightier, dry frame; Muscat smells of the grape itself and is lighter.

cards.front: Muscat Blanc: give its Italian name and its two wines from Asti.
cards.back: Moscato Bianco. Moscato d'Asti is sweet and gently sparkling at about five per cent alcohol; Asti is the fully sparkling wine of the same grape.

cards.front: Muscat Blanc blind: Asti or Rutherglen, what tips it?
cards.back: Pale colour, fresh grape, orange blossom and low alcohol lean Asti. Amber to brown, with raisin, dried fig and toffee and the warmth of spirit, leans Rutherglen.

cards.front: How does a Muscat vin doux naturel keep its sweetness?
cards.back: Grape spirit is added part way through fermentation. It stops the yeast, leaves the grape's sugar in the wine and lifts the alcohol to 15 per cent or more.

questions.q: A sweet wine poured blind is deep amber brown and luscious, with raisin, dried fig and toffee and the warmth of added spirit. Which origin fits it?
questions.exp: Years in old casks in a hot, dry region turn Rutherglen Muscat brown and give it raisin and toffee. Moscato d'Asti is pale, fresh and low in alcohol, with no spirit added.

questions.q: A guest wants something light, sweet and gently fizzy with a peach tart, and as little alcohol as possible. Which wine do you bring?
questions.exp: Moscato d'Asti is sweet and gently sparkling at about five per cent alcohol. Beaumes-de-Venise and Rutherglen Muscat are fortified with spirit, and Sauternes is still, rich and far stronger.

questions.q: A guest loves the scent of Muscat but does not want a sweet wine. From which region do you choose a bottle?
questions.exp: Alsace ferments its Muscat dry: the same fresh grape scent with a crisp finish. Asti, Beaumes-de-Venise and Samos are known for sweet Muscat.

sources.title: Rhône Valley Vineyards: Muscat de Beaumes-de-Venise, vin doux naturel
University of California, Davis: Muscat blanc

report: Mode contrast, as the plan fixes it, with Asti, the French vins doux naturels, Alsace and Samos against Rutherglen and California. The difference is as much one of method as of world, fresh and early bottled against fortified and cask aged, and the blur line says so; a second reader may prefer at home and abroad.
No respelling stands in the Court's grid; the say line gives the French name and then the Italian.

Rutherglen, Samos and Constantia are written from the Codex's own region records (the red skinned Brown Muscat raisined on the vine, fortified and aged in old wood in hot sheds; Samos Nectar dried, cask aged and amber), so no new source is listed for them.

California: the Davis variety sheet says Muscat blanc there goes mostly into sweet, light wines, some sparkling, and that Muscat Canelli is the common local name. Much bottled Moscato in California may come from other Muscats, which the guest answer admits.
The service temperature follows the Codex's rows for sweet whites and light sparkling; the Codex's Rutherglen record says pour the Muscat cool, in small glasses.

Left out: the age bands of the Rutherglen classification, where the Codex's card and the growers' own figures differ slightly (about 3 to 5, 6 to 10, 11 to 19 and 20 years in the Codex; two to five, five to twelve, twelve to twenty and twenty or more in the growers' material read here). A checker may wish to look at that card.

Left out: any claim about how old the Muscat family is beyond old; and Piedmont's hazelnut cake and panettone with Moscato d'Asti, widely repeated and not read on the consortium's own page in this session.
The sources were read through search results; this session could not open the hosts directly.

checked.verdict: Sound after five fixes. Moscato d'Asti (stopped at about five per cent, capped at six and a half), Muscat Canelli as the California name, and Rutherglen's red skinned Muscat raisined on the vine were confirmed.
changed: glass.ladder: Alsace stood on the moderate rung beside Asti. The Court's grid read calls Alsace cool, so it has a cool rung of its own, where it is fermented dry: fresh table grape, elderflower and lemon.
lines.s45: gentle stood twice in two sentences; the sparkle is now light.
lines.s45, the closing line: about half the alcohol of most wines is now less than half. At about five per cent, and never above six and a half, it is under half of a table wine's twelve to fourteen.

worlds.contrast.why: early bottling does not keep alcohol low. The hillsides keep the perfume fresh, and the fermentation stopped early keeps the alcohol low, as the entry's own cellar line and third guest answer say.
compare, the Torrontés tell: the grapey, flowery nose is now the grapey nose; flowery is a family word in disguise.
open: The mode: the contrast is of method as much as of world, as the author says. It stands because Rutherglen Muscat and California Moscato are styles a guest meets on a list, and the blur line admits the rest.
The entry reads in 898 words of 900.
The Rutherglen age bands stay out of the entry. The growers' own material says age is one factor among several; the figures on the Codex's card are the ones the trade repeats.
